D1.question: What public price should the Daily Planner carry for the first 30 days?

reasons: $17 is the only owner-approved price, and any change is owner-gated, so holding avoids an unapproved public change.
A handful of sales cannot separate $14, $17 and $24 (aut:F05, aut:F06), so a price move would be guesswork rather than tested evidence.
At $17 the $100 payout gate needs 8 sales, one fewer than at $14, and the net is $14.01 per direct sale versus $11.39 at $14.
$24 sits well above the nearest anchor, Rootlyn at $14.99 for 24 pages, and far above the $1-$10 volume shops, with no reviews or audience yet to justify it.
risks: $17 may be high relative to $1-$10 volume files, so conversion from warm traffic could be weak.
The 427-page Daily Planner has no reviews, so buyers may anchor on the 0-review $17 calendar as a signal of low demand.
The audience skews UK, Australia and Canada, so a USD price may create friction, and holding $17 does not resolve that.
Gumroad Discover needs a first sale and a roughly 3-week review, so early sales may stay thin regardless of price.
Only about $5 of marketing budget and no paid ads means traffic may be too small to read any price signal in 30 days.
answers.first_test: With owner approval, publish the Daily Planner at $17 and keep it fixed for 30 days. Track link-in-bio clicks, checkout starts and sales against the ~350-view-per-post proxy, and log any refunds under the 30-day policy. Revisit price only if there is enough traffic to compare outcomes.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence from owner-approved tests or real checkout data showing a clear conversion gap between price points at a meaningful sample, or a confirmed USD price problem for UK, Australia and Canada buyers. Either would justify an owner-approved change, with $14 favored if conversion is weak and $24 only if the product gains reviews and demand.

reasons: $17 is the only owner-approved price, and changing a public price is owner-gated, so holding avoids an unapproved change.
Net per direct sale is highest at $17 ($14.01) versus $11.39 at $14; stepping down lowers margin without evidence it would lift volume.
The $100 payout gate needs 8 sales at $17 versus 9 at $14, so $14 makes the first payout harder to reach.
A handful of sales cannot separate prices, so a price test in 30 days would yield no reliable signal; holding keeps the variable fixed while traffic is built.
risks: Rootlyn at $14.99 for 24 pages suggests $17 for 427 pages may look expensive to some buyers, possibly depressing conversion.
With no reviews and no audience yet, few sales may occur at any price, so the $17 anchor may go unseen.
A USD price may mismatch a UK/Australia/Canada audience, a question this decision does not resolve.
Holding may leave the product unpublished or unsold for 30 days regardless, so the price choice has limited near-term impact.
answers.first_test: Owner approves publishing at $17 USD, adds the payout method, and tracks views-to-click and click-to-sale on the link-in-bio for 30 days, with a checklist opt-in as the top-of-funnel signal before any price change.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence from the owner's own warm traffic (for example, at least a few checkout-page visits per sale at $17 showing price objection, or competitor evidence in the target market showing sales at lower prices) would justify revisiting a step down; a currency or regional pricing decision would also reopen the question.

D2.question: What is the first thing cold viewers are asked to take?
options: Free Sample Week of the planner

reasons: The free 7-day checklist already exists, so it can be published with no new build or extra compliance read, which fits the 6-hour week 2 and 4-5 hour weekly limits.
Cold viewers have no reason to buy a $17 planner before trust exists; a free opt-in is the lowest-friction first ask.
A list is the only way to re-reach viewers, and Gumroad email stays locked until the first payout, so the checklist is the sole route to repeat contact.
The stated default (paid_every = 3, checklist first) is already the engine setting, and the Sample Week option is a candidate that needs a build and second compliance read.
risks: Opt-in conversion may fall roughly 74% under confirmed opt-in, so list growth could be slow.
Mixed-traffic opt-in figures are creator-reported and weak; the sales-page 1-2% figure comes from a 2014 dataset.
Planner sales may stay near zero while the checklist is the only live offer, and the $17 planner has no reviews and is unpublished.
US audience is absent from the data, so UK/AU/CA-weighted assumptions may not hold.
answers.first_test: Publish the free 7-day checklist as the first link-in-bio ask for cold viewers, with the planner shown as every third paid offer; over 30 days track opt-in rate from ~52,500 projected Shorts views (or actual views), and check whether any opt-ins reach the planner, using only the $5 budget and no paid ads.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that opt-in pages from this audience convert far below the stated range while direct sales pages convert materially higher, or a Sample Week build and compliance read completed early enough that a free sample-based magnet can launch without slipping the weekly hour limits.

reasons: The free 7-day checklist already exists, so it can be used on day one without a new build or second compliance read.
A free, low-commitment first ask suits cold viewers from Shorts, and it creates the only route to re-reach them, since Gumroad email stays locked until the first payout.
The Daily Planner is an unpublished draft and not yet approved for public use, so it cannot be the day-one ask.
The Sample Week was deferred for build and compliance reasons; the current default already matches the constraints of a 6-hour week and a $5 budget.
risks: Opt-in conversion is uncertain: the 4% figure is on mixed traffic, and the one cited study suggests confirmed opt-in can cut conversion by roughly 74%.
Reach is small: about 52,500 views in 30 days is a proxy, and link-in-bio is the only clickable path, so few viewers may reach the hub.
The checklist-first ask could attract lead-magnet seekers who never buy, leaving the planner with little warm audience.
The audience data is skewed (18-24, mostly female, UK/AU/CA) and US performance is unverified, which may affect which offer resonates.
answers.first_test: For 30 days, keep the free checklist as the first ask on all link-in-bio traffic, paid_every = 3, and 5 Shorts/day. Track link-in-bio visits, checklist opt-in rate, and the share of opt-ins who later view the planner. Compare against the 4% prior and stop or revise if opt-in is far below it.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: I would switch if the owner approves and compliance clears a Sample Week build that can be produced within the time budget, or if opt-in data shows the checklist is converting well below the 4% prior while a planner-first page gets measurably more sales from social traffic.

D3.question: Which product should lead, and what is the second ask if the warm launch is weak?
options: Planner plus Debt planner as two listings

reasons: The Daily Planner is the only product that is built, owner-approved and priced at $17, so it can be listed soonest with no new compliance review.
The Debt Payoff Planner is a spreadsheet that is not owner-approved and would add hours plus a second review of credit and debt wording, which the 4-5 hour weekly budget cannot absorb.
Printables at $9 fit the Etsy volume band, but the format evidence favors Sheets, Notion and GoodNotes files over a printable PDF planner, and the $9 product is not built.
Traffic is only a proxy of about 350 views per post, so a single approved product gives a cleaner read on the warm launch than splitting attention across two listings.
risks: A 427-page Daily Planner at $17 with no reviews may sell little regardless of cover, and the Gumroad Discover path needs a $100 balance and a first sale before any traction.
The Daily Planner is a printable PDF, a format the evidence rates as less proven than Sheets or Notion files.
Gumroad payouts need $100 and a 7-day hold, and nothing is live until a payout method is added, so revenue timing is uncertain.
Conversion priors of 1.5-7% are creator-reported and weak; the audience data is unverified for the US.
answers.first_test: Once the owner approves, publish the Daily Planner at $17 on Gumroad with the free 7-day checklist linked from the hub, and send the warm launch to the existing link-in-bio traffic from the first week's Shorts, tracking views, checklist sign-ups and sales over Days 1-14.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: If the warm launch shows checklist sign-ups but no sales by Day 10-14, or if the Debt planner draft is approved and its 7-day sample performs better, I would switch the second ask to the Debt Payoff Planner or to a Sheets-format printable at $9 rather than a second PDF.

reasons: The Daily Planner is the only product that is built, owner-approved at $17, and nets $14.01 per direct Gumroad sale, so it can go live soonest.
The Debt Payoff Planner is an unapproved spreadsheet that would add hours and a second compliance review on credit and debt wording, which the 4-5 hour weekly budget cannot absorb.
Printables at $9 fit the $1-$10 volume band, but the printable PDF planner format is less proven than Sheets, Notion and GoodNotes files, and switching would discard the approved asset.
With about 350 views per post and no audience yet, a single clear listing gives the warm launch a clean read rather than splitting the small traffic across two products.
risks: A $17 365-day style planner with no reviews may sell little regardless of cover, and Gumroad Discover requires a first sale and ~3 week review.
Nothing is live until the payout method is added and the $100 payout threshold is reached, so revenue timing is uncertain.
Format evidence favors Sheets/Notion/GoodNotes files, so the PDF planner may underperform against expectations.
Conversion priors of 1.5-7% are weak creator-reported figures, and the US audience is unverified.
answers.first_test: Publish the Daily Planner listing once the owner approves, add the payout method, and drive the 7-day checklist link from link-in-bio across the first 30 days of Shorts, tracking views-to-checklist signups and checklist-to-planner sales.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: If the warm launch shows weak checklist signups or zero planner sales by Day 10-14 (trigger X11), or if buyer evidence shows demand for debt content or a Sheets/Notion-format product, I would switch the second ask to the Debt Payoff Planner or a printable at $9 respectively.

D4.question: After the warm launch, which stranger channel gets the owner's scarce hours first (Days 8-30)?

reasons: Etsy is the only channel in the facts where strangers actively search to buy, so it is the only stranger channel that does not depend on first building an audience.

The recommended default already puts the Etsy edition first in Days 8-14, and the owner's roughly 6 hours in week 2 can cover the recompression and link-free file work without opening several channels at once.
TikTok/Reels cannot carry a profile link below 1,000 followers and averages about 350 views, so cross-posts would spend hours on traffic that cannot convert on the spot.
Creator commissions net $8.41 per sale with unmeasured acceptance, so their payoff is too uncertain to justify scarce hours ahead of a channel with a known buyer search.
risks: Zero reviews against incumbents with thousands means the listing may get little search visibility regardless of quality.
Etsy approval is not confirmed, so the hours could be spent on a listing that cannot go live on schedule.
Recompressing the 427-page PDF and producing a link-free edition may take longer than the week-2 budget.
The $5 marketing budget cannot buy reviews or promotion, so early sales may be near zero.
answers.first_test: Within Days 8-14, produce one link-free, recompressed Etsy edition of the Daily Planner with a sample-page preview, publish it only after owner approval, and track 7 days of search impressions, views and favorites with no paid promotion.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: If Etsy approval is refused or the listing gets near-zero search impressions after 7 days, or if creator acceptance data shows a real commission pipeline, I would move hours to creator pitches instead.

reasons: Etsy is the only channel where strangers actively search to buy, so it is the only option that targets purchase intent rather than hoping for reach.
The recommended default already sequences the Etsy edition into wave 1 (Days 8-14), which fits the 6-hour week-2 budget better than opening everything at once.

The other options are weaker on current facts: TikTok/Reels averages about 350 views and has no profile link below 1,000 followers, the YouTube bridge needs advanced features and has no click-through benchmark, and creator acceptance is unmeasured.
The $5 marketing budget and no-paid-ads constraint rule out buying Etsy traffic, so the owner's hours are the main lever on this channel.
risks: Etsy is not approved yet, so the channel may not open within Days 8-14 and the hours could be lost to waiting.
Zero reviews against incumbents with thousands means the listing may sell little regardless of cover quality.
Files must be recompressed and a link-free edition built, which could consume more of the 6-hour week than estimated.
Incumbent Etsy sellers price planners and sheets at $1-$10, so a $17 listing faces price resistance.
Conversion and traffic on Etsy are unmeasured, so the decision rests on qualitative fit rather than observed sales.
answers.first_test: Within Days 8-10, list one link-free Etsy edition of the Daily Planner (after approval and file recompression) and track views, favorites and sales over 14 days against a fixed threshold, such as at least one sale or a clear listing-view signal, before allocating more hours.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: If Etsy approval is not granted by Day 10, or if the link-free edition cannot be produced within about 2 hours, I would shift the hours to the owner's TikTok/Reels cross-posts or the creator pitches. I would also reconsider if the owner's own Shorts show clicks to the link-in-bio hub that suggest warm traffic is converting better than any stranger channel.

D6.question: What launch mechanic goes in the warm personal messages?

reasons: The product is an unpublished draft with no public launch approved, so any mechanic needs the owner's yes first. A plain no-discount message is the smallest change to approve.
FIRST14 is a price change. It nets $11.39 instead of $14.01 and pushes the $100 Discover/payout gate from about 8 sales to 9, which slows the one milestone that unlocks payouts and email workflows.
The facts give no evidence that a discount converts better. Conversion priors are creator-reported and weak, and a handful of sales cannot test $14 against $17.
With about 6 hours in week 2 and only $5 of marketing budget, a discount adds a deadline to track and a code to manage without a demonstrated benefit.
risks: Warm contacts may convert less without a reason to act now, so early sales could stay slow.
Without a deadline, the message may get ignored or put off.
If the owner wants urgency, a real-deadline code can be added later as a separate, approved decision.
answers.first_test: Send 10-20 personal messages to warm contacts with the $17 link and a short, honest note about what the planner covers. Track link clicks and sales for 7 days, then compare the response rate with the earlier draft messages, if any.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: I would switch to FIRST14 with a real end date if the owner approves a price change and warm contacts show clear hesitation about $17, or if the owner accepts the slower route to the $100 gate in exchange for a faster start. I would choose Free Sample Week if the owner wants to build trust first and can produce a sample within the time budget.

reasons: FIRST14 needs the owner's yes because it is a price change, and it nets $11.39 per sale versus $14.01 at $17, so it adds cost without a tested benefit.
A handful of sales cannot show whether $14 beats $17, so a discount buys a launch bump, not learning.
Free Sample Week produces no sales toward the $100 Gumroad gate and costs owner time on a 427-page product with only about 6 hours in week 2.
Nothing is live yet (payout method not added), so the first priority is a clean, honest launch at the owner-approved $17 price.
risks: Warm contacts may not buy at $17, so the $100 gate could take much longer to reach.
Without a reason to act now, the warm messages may get little response.
Skipping the discount forgoes a possible early-sales push that the owner may want.
No reviews means limited sales regardless of the message, so the launch may stay slow.
answers.first_test: After the owner approves going public, send a short personal message with the $17 Gumroad link to a small set of warm contacts, track clicks and sales for 14 days, and note any replies that mention price or timing.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: If the owner approves a price change and a real end date, and warm contacts indicate they would only buy with a code, switch to FIRST14, since the 9-sale gate would still be reachable from warm contacts.

D7.question: How should the Escape the Rat Race series be handled for the next 90 days?
options: Free checklist only, 1 slot a day, under the written rule
Pause until a copy gate clears

answers.choice: Free checklist only, 1 slot a day, under the written rule
reasons: Gumroad's terms ban unsubstantiated earnings claims on any channel the seller controls, and the series rests on passive-income and get-rich-style framing, so the planner offer cannot be attached safely.
The Daily Planner is unpublished and not live, and the payout method is not added, so there is no offer that can truthfully sit behind this series yet.
Limiting the series to 1 of 5 daily slots with a free-checklist CTA keeps exposure small while the phrase gate and research-brief rule are tested.
Using only education framing, no income language, and named figures only as sourced subjects with a not-affiliated line matches the business's no-advice and no-income-claims rules.
risks: Platform policy conflicts (YouTube spam page, TikTok, MailerLite) are unresolved, so a flag or notice could hit the whole channel.
Named figures such as Hormozi, Kiyosaki and Peña could be read as implied endorsement even with a disclaimer.
Holding scripts that fail the phrase gate may leave slots empty and reduce output with a 4-5 hour weekly budget.
Limited reach: a single slot a day with no audience yet gives little signal, and the series may feel templated despite the variety goal.
answers.first_test: Write one Escape the Rat Race script in plain education language, run it through the phrase gate and the research brief for any named figure, add the not-affiliated line, and post it once in the 1-slot free-checklist CTA slot; hold it if any phrase fails rather than softening it.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: A written reply from Gumroad or the platforms confirming that this series framing is allowed, or a flag or notice that would instead justify pausing the series entirely (option 2); or a published, approved planner with substantiated, non-earnings claims that would make option 3 viable.

answers.choice: Free checklist only, 1 slot a day, under the written rule
reasons: The planner offer attached would send the series toward the Gumroad and platform language risks, since the Terms ban unsubstantiated earnings claims and the series relies on passive-income framing.
The Daily Planner is an unpublished draft with no payout method and no live Gumroad sale, so attaching it now adds risk without any delivery path.
One slot a day is about 30 posts a month at most, which fits the 4-5 hours a week after launch and keeps the channel's variety goal (cmp:F2) partly intact.
Pausing entirely would stop learning, while a free-checklist-only CTA keeps the series testable under the phrase gate and the written rule.
risks: Phrase-gate holds may leave slots empty, which makes the 1-slot-a-day cadence hard to sustain on a thin budget.
Source-based research briefs for named figures (Hormozi, Kiyosaki, Peña) take time within 6 hours and may delay scripts.
Platform interpretation is unsettled (YouTube spam page is a hypothesis), so a notice could arrive mid-test.
The free checklist still drives little revenue without an audience, so the series may not justify the effort.
answers.first_test: Draft 5 Escape the Rat Race scripts with no passive-income, side-income-amount, quit-your-job, financial-freedom or get-rich language, each with a free-checklist CTA and a not-affiliated line for any named person. Run the phrase gate, hold any failure, post at most 1 per day for 2 weeks, and log holds, views and checklist sign-ups.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: A written compliance check confirming that the series framing and named-figure references are allowed on Gumroad, TikTok, YouTube and MailerLite, or a live published planner with a payout method and clear terms that permit a planner offer, would justify attaching the planner offer. A platform notice or flag would push me to pause.

D10.question: Should the owner opt the product out of Gumroad's global affiliate program (10%) once it is Discover-eligible?
options: Opt out for the first 90 days
Decide at the Day-30 review with the first sales data

answers.choice: Decide at the Day-30 review with the first sales data
reasons: Discover eligibility needs a $100 balance, a ~3 week review and a first sale, so the affiliate program cannot take effect before about Day 30; deciding now is premature.
The facts give no sales, conversion, or affiliate-performance data, so an opt-out for 90 days or staying in are both chosen without evidence.
Opting out is reversible, so deferring the choice to Day 30 loses little while keeping the option to use affiliates if they prove useful.

Uncontrolled affiliate endorsements carry advertiser liability and the brand is education-only with no income claims, so the risk is real and should be weighed against actual data rather than assumed.
risks: Deferring may lead to auto-enrolment at the 10% rate running unmonitored for days before the review if the setting is not checked at listing.
Without a pre-set rule, the owner may default to staying opted in by inaction, exposing the brand to uncontrolled claims.
Day-30 data may be too thin (few or no sales) to be a meaningful basis for the decision.
answers.first_test: Before listing goes live, check the Gumroad affiliate setting and record the owner's default; at Day 30, review whether any affiliate-attributed sales or claims exist and whether any affiliate content breaches the no-income-claims and education-only rules.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: If the owner confirms that affiliate enrolment can be set to off at listing without losing Discover eligibility, I would recommend opting out from day one; if affiliate sales are shown to be substantial and the content can be reviewed, I would lean to staying in.

answers.choice: Decide at the Day-30 review with the first sales data
reasons: Discover eligibility needs $100 balance, a ~3 week review and a first sale, so the affiliate setting cannot matter before about Day 30; deciding now is premature.
The facts give no sales, conversion or affiliate-performance data, so an opt-out versus stay-in choice made today would be a guess.
Opting out is reversible, so waiting to Day 30 loses little, and the review gives real data on whether Discover traffic and uncontrolled promoters are worth the 10% fee.
Uncontrolled affiliate endorsements carry liability for the advertiser (cmp:F13), so the owner should decide with a clear view of what promoters are saying, which the Day-30 review can provide.
risks: Waiting may leave the product auto-enrolled at 10% for a short window after eligibility, a small cost if promoters begin posting unmonitored claims.
If the owner does not schedule the Day-30 review, the default setting persists by inertia.
The recommendation to opt out for 90 days is reasonable on liability grounds, and deferring could drift past the point where it is easy to act.
answers.first_test: Once Discover eligibility is reached, check the affiliate setting and log every promoter post and claim; at the Day-30 review, compare affiliate-attributed sales and any compliance flags against direct sales before deciding.
answers.what_would_change_my_mind: If the owner's review shows affiliate sales meaningfully outperform direct sales with no problematic claims, or if the owner can monitor promoter posts within 48 hours at low cost, I would stay opted in; if any uncontrolled promoter makes income-type or unsubstantiated claims, I would opt out immediately.
